summary: Discusses differences between the IS-IS routing protocol as written in ISO 10589 and the way it is actually deployed. It is meant to help people who implement, test and deploy IS-IS. A companion document, RFC 3787, covers the IP-routing side described in RFC 1195.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3719 is a list of differences between the IS-IS routing protocol as specified in ISO 10589 and the version that routers actually run. It covers timers that the standard fixed but networks changed, values the standard left variable but nobody varies, and several cases where the standard's behaviour turned out to be disruptive in practice. Each item comes with a recommendation for implementers.

questions: how does is-is differ from iso 10589
subtitle: Where the IS-IS protocol as written down differs from the IS-IS that routers actually run

tldr.problem: IS-IS was written down in ISO 10589, but real networks and real implementations have drifted away from that document in a dozen small ways, and two routers that disagree about one of them will not talk properly.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists the differences and gives a recommendation for each one: which values to change, which to keep, and what an implementation must check when it receives a packet.
tldr.outcome: The recommendations are concrete, such as using a System ID of 6 bytes and a maximumAreaAddresses value of 3, and treating an LSP with a zero checksum as corrupt rather than purging it. The memo adds no new security concerns of its own.

facts.label: LSP database size at each level

today: RFC 3719 is an Informational memo from February 2004 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It gives no protocol of its own, and its security considerations section says the clarifications raise no new security concerns because there is no change in the underlying protocol described in ISO 10589.

sections.title: Why This Memo Exists
sections.content:
Interior Gateway Protocols such as IS-IS are designed to provide timely information about the best routes in a routing domain. The original design of IS-IS, as described in ISO 10589, has proved to be quite durable, but a number of original design choices have been modified. This document addresses the differences between the protocol described in ISO 10589 and the protocol that can be observed on the wire today, as a service to those implementing, testing and deploying IS-IS. A companion document covers the differences between the protocol described in RFC 1195 for routing IP traffic and current practice.

The differences fall into three groups. Some parameters that ISO 10589 defined as constant are modified in practice, such as MaxAge, the lifetime of a Link State PDU, the ISISHoldingMultiplier used to describe the generation of hello packets, and ReceiveLSPBufferSize. Some values that ISO 10589 defined as variables do not vary in practice, such as the ID Length that defines the length of the System ID, maximumAreaAddresses, and the protocol version. The rest are behaviours where the standard's rule turned out to be disruptive or ambiguous, and the memo gives a different rule.

The memo opens with the observation that in theory there is no difference between theory and practice, but in practice there is. It is explicit that the key words MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT and MAY are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: The standard was written once and has held up well, but networks and software have moved past it in small ways. This memo lists where they differ so that two routers built by different people still agree.

sections.title: Constants That Are Variable
sections.content:
Each LSP contains a RemainingLifetime field, initially set to the MaxAge value on the generating router. The value is decremented to mark the passage of time and the number of times it has been forwarded, and when the value of a foreign LSP becomes zero the router starts a purging process that flushes the LSP from the network, so that corrupted or otherwise invalid LSPs do not remain in the network indefinitely. The rate at which LSPs are regenerated by the originating router is set by maximumLSPGenerationInterval.

MaxAge is defined in ISO 10589 as an architectural constant of 20 minutes, and it is recommended that maximumLSPGenerationInterval be set to 15 minutes. These times have proved too short in some networks, as they result in a steady flow of LSP updates even when nothing is changing, so some implementations let the network operator set them. If MaxAge is smaller than maximumLSPGenerationInterval, an LSP will expire before it is replaced, and because RemainingLifetime is decremented each time the LSP is forwarded, an LSP far from its origin appears older and is removed sooner. MaxAge should therefore exceed maximumLSPGenerationInterval by at least ZeroAgeLifetime plus minimumLSPTransmissionInterval, the first being an estimate of how long it takes to flood an LSP through the network and the second taking account of how long a router might delay before sending one. The original recommendation was that MaxAge be at least 5 minutes larger, and that recommendation is still valid today. An implementation may use a MaxAge greater than 1200 seconds, should exceed maximumLSPGenerationInterval by at least 300 seconds, and should not use its MaxAge value to discard LSPs from peers. It is also not required to coordinate the RemainingLifetime it assigns with the values it accepts, and it must ignore the ISO 10589 sentence that a received LSP with a Remaining Lifetime greater than MaxAge is to be processed as if there were a checksum error.

ISISHoldingMultiplier is used to generate hello packets. An IS sends hello PDUs on a periodic basis over active circuits so that other attached routers can monitor its aliveness. The hello includes a two byte Holding Time field defining the time to live of an adjacency, and if no hello arrives within that time the neighbour is assumed to be no longer operational and the adjacency is removed. ISO 10589 defines ISISHoldingMultiplier to be 10, which implies that a neighbour must lose 10 hellos before an adjacency times out. In practice a value of 10 has proved too large. DECnet Phase V defined two related values: holdingMultiplier, with a default of 3, for point-to-point hellos, and ISISHoldingMultiplier, with a default of 10, for LAN hellos. Most implementations today set the default ISISHoldingMultiplier to 3 for both circuit types, and adjacent systems may use different Holding Time values and still form an adjacency with non-symmetric hold times. An implementation may allow ISISHoldingMultiplier to be configurable, but values lower than 3 are unstable and may cause adjacencies to flap.
sections.plainLanguage: Two timers have moved away from the standard. The LSP lifetime of 20 minutes is often set by the operator instead, and the multiplier used to work out how long a neighbour has to be silent is 3 in practice rather than the 10 the standard says.

sections.title: Variables That Are Constant
sections.content:
The ID Length is a field carried in all PDUs, and defines the length of the System ID. It is allowed to take values from 0 to 8, and a value of 0 is interpreted as a length of 6 bytes. It is easy to use an Ethernet MAC address to generate a unique 6 byte System ID, and since the System ID only has significance within the IGP domain, 6 bytes has proved easy to use and ample in practice. There are also new IS-IS Traffic Engineering TLVs which assume a 6 byte System ID. An implementation must use an ID Length of 6 and must check the ID Length in the IS-IS PDUs it receives; if a router encounters a PDU with an ID Length different from 0 or 6 it must discard the PDU and should generate a notification, iDFieldLengthMismatch in ISO 10589 and isisIDLenMismatch in the IS-IS MIB.

maximumAreaAddresses is an integer between 1 and 254 defining the number of synonymous Area Addresses that can be in use in a Level 1 area, and it is advertised in the header of each IS-IS PDU. Most deployed networks use one Area Address for a Level 1 area; a second is required for a seamless transition when areas are merged or split, and the third was originally required to support DECnet Phase IV addresses as well as OSI addresses during a transition. ISO 10589 requires that all routers in an area or domain use a consistent value, and common practice is to use the value 3, so an implementation that only supports 3 can expect to interoperate successfully with other conformant systems. ISO 10589 also specifies that an advertised value of 0 is treated as equivalent to 3. An implementation should use the value 3 and should check the value advertised in the PDUs it receives; if it receives a PDU with a value that is neither 0 nor 3 it must discard the PDU and should generate a notification, maximumAreaAddressMismatch in ISO 10589 and isisMaxAreaAddressesMismatch in the IS-IS MIB.

The protocol version appears in two one-byte fields in the headers, Version/Protocol ID Extension and Version. An implementation should set both to 1 and should check them in received PDUs; if a router receives a PDU with a value other than 1 for either field it must drop the packet and should generate the isisVersionSkew notification.

On metrics, ISO 10589 describes four: Default, Delay, Expense and Error. None but the Default Metric are used in deployed networks, and most implementations consider only the Default Metric. In ISO 10589 the most significant bit of the 8-bit metric was the field S, used to say whether the metric was meaningful, and it was always 0 for the Default Metric, which must always be supported. RFC 2966 uses this bit in the Default Metric to mark Level 1 routes that have been leaked from Level 1 to Level 2 and back down into Level 1 again. Implementations must generate the Default Metric when using narrow metrics and should ignore the other three, and must assume that the Default Metric is supported even if the S bit is set.
sections.plainLanguage: Three settings that the standard left open are in fact always the same: a 6-byte System ID, three area addresses, and version 1. A router should check these and drop anything that disagrees.

sections.title: ReceiveLSPBufferSize
sections.content:
Because IS-IS does not allow segmentation of protocol PDUs, LSPs must be propagated without modification on every IS-IS enabled link throughout the area or domain. It is therefore essential to configure a maximum size that all routers can forward, receive and store. This affects the largest LSP a router can receive, the size of the largest LSP it can generate through the originatingL1LSPBufferSize and originatingL2LSPBufferSize parameters, and the available Link MTU for supported circuits, which often differs from the MTU available to IP clients.

ISO 10589 defines the architectural constant ReceiveLSPBufferSize with the value 1492 bytes, along with the two private management parameters for the originating buffer sizes. The crucial relationships are that the originating buffer sizes must not exceed ReceiveLSPBufferSize, and that for all Level 1 links in the area and all Level 2 links in the domain the originating buffer size must not exceed the MTU. The original thought was that operators could decrease the originating buffer size when dealing with smaller MTUs, but would not need to increase ReceiveLSPBufferSize beyond 1492.

With new information to be advertised in LSPs, such as the Traffic Engineering TLVs, the limited space of the LSP database that may be generated by each router, 256 times 1492 bytes at each level, has become an issue. Given that modern networks with MTUs larger than 1492 on all links are not uncommon, one way to expand the database is to allow values of ReceiveLSPBufferSize greater than 1492. This must be done with care: if any system in the network does not support values larger than 1492, or if one or more link MTUs used by IS-IS anywhere in the area or domain is smaller than the largest LSP which may be generated by any router, then full propagation of all LSPs may not be possible, resulting in routing loops and black holes.

The memo recommends six steps when changing the value: set ReceiveLSPBufferSize to a consistent value throughout the network; do not enable IS-IS on circuits which do not support an MTU at least as large as the originating buffer size at the appropriate level; include an originatingLSPBufferSize TLV when generating LSPs; when receiving LSPs, check for that TLV and report values larger than the local ReceiveLSPBufferSize through the defined notifications and alarms; report the receipt of a PDU larger than the local ReceiveLSPBufferSize through the same route; and do not discard large PDUs by default, since storing and processing them as normal PDUs may help maintain coherence in a misconfigured network. The first two steps are enough by themselves, but the consequences of a mismatch are serious enough and difficult enough to detect that the rest are recommended to help track down and correct problems.

The memo also deals with padding of hello PDUs. To prevent the establishment of adjacencies between systems which may not be able to receive and propagate IS-IS PDUs due to inconsistent buffer settings, ISO 10589 requires padding on point-to-point links, where the initial hello is padded to the maximum of the link MTU and the relevant originating buffer size. The standard assumed that a failed delivery would disconnect the subnetwork connection in both directions and be reported to both systems, so that a padded PDU which was too big to receive would reset the link. Link layer protocols in use on point-to-point circuits today often lack that service, and the initial padded PDU might be silently dropped without resetting the circuit. An implementation using padding should therefore pad point-to-point hello PDUs until the sender declares the adjacency to be Up, should resume transmitting padded hellos whenever the adjacency is torn down, and should bring adjacencies down and reestablish them if the originating buffer sizes are modified. Some implementations choose not to pad, and padding does not provide a transitive relation: if A and B can form an adjacency and B and C can form one, that does not mean A and C could.
sections.plainLanguage: IS-IS cannot split a message, so every router has to be able to pass the largest one along. The standard's 1492-byte limit is now often raised, but only if every router and every link in the area can handle the larger size, or messages get lost and routes loop.

sections.title: Bad Checksums and Duplicate LSPs
sections.content:
A checksum of 0 is impossible if the checksum is computed according to the rules of ISO 8473. ISO 10589 states that an LSP received with a zero checksum shall be treated as if the Remaining Lifetime were zero, with the age overwritten with zero, which directs the receiver to purge the LSP. This has proved disruptive in practice, and an implementation should treat all LSPs with a zero checksum and a non-zero remaining lifetime as if they had a checksum error, discarding them.

The same applies to LSPs received with an invalid PDU checksum. ISO 10589:2002 requires that a router receiving an LSP with an incorrect checksum or invalid syntax should generate a corruptedLSPReceived circuit event and discard the PDU. While the earlier wording required purging, that has been found to be disruptive, and most implementations today follow the revised specification and simply drop the LSP.

On point-to-point links, ISO 10589 does not explicitly require comparing the source ID of a received hello with the neighbourSystemID of an existing adjacency. Implementations should make that comparison and delete the adjacency if they differ. Because the hellos as specified carry no checksum, a corrupted hello may falsely indicate a change in the neighbour's System ID, and a link with frequent errors could cause an adjacency to flap. An optional checksum TLV may be used to detect such corruption, and hellos carrying that TLV that are corrupted should be silently dropped rather than dropping the adjacency. Some implementations instead discard received hellos whose source ID differs from the neighbourSystemID, which may prevent needless flapping caused by undetected corruption, at the cost of having to wait for the adjacency to time out when a real administrative change to the neighbour's System ID has happened.

When a router shuts down it may leave old LSPs in the network, and a rebooting system normally flushes them out by reissuing those fragments with a higher sequence number or by purging fragments it is no longer generating. In the case where a received LSP or SNP entry and an LSP in the local database have the same LSP ID, the same sequence number and non-zero remaining lifetimes, but different non-zero checksums, the rules of ISO 10589 cannot determine which of the two is newer. An implementation may opt to break the tie by comparing the checksums, and if it does so it must consider the entry with the higher checksum to be newer, treating the checksum field as a 16-bit unsigned integer in network byte order. The choice of the higher rather than the lower checksum is arbitrary, but it aligns with existing implementations and ensures compatibility. A purged LSP, that is one with a remaining lifetime of zero, is always considered newer than a non-purged copy of the same LSP.
sections.plainLanguage: The standard's rule for a damaged LSP was to flush it from the network, which caused disruption, so it should just be dropped. When two copies of the same LSP disagree, the one with the higher checksum wins.

sections.title: Complete CSNP Sets and the Overload Bit
sections.content:
There are several cases in which a complete set of CSNPs must be generated: the DIS on a LAN, two routers peering over a point-to-point link, and a router helping another router perform graceful restart. ISO 10589 defines a complete set of CSNPs as a set whose start and end LSP ID ranges cover the complete possible range of LSP IDs, so that no possible LSP ID value falls outside the range of one of the CSNPs in the set. Strict adherence is required to ensure the reliability of the update process, since deviation can lead to subtle and hard to detect defects. It is not sufficient to send a set of CSNPs which merely covers the range of LSP IDs in the local database.

The memo gives an example. If the current Level 1 LSP database on a router consists of non pseudo-node LSPs from system 1111.1111.1111 numbered 0 to 89 and from system 2222.2222.2222 numbered 0 to 89, and the maximum size of a CSNP is 1492 bytes so that 90 CSNP entries fit into a single PDU, then a correctly formatted complete set runs from 0000.0000.0000.00-00 to 1111.1111.1111.00-59 and then from 1111.1111.1111.00-5A to FFFF.FFFF.FFFF.FF-FF. A set that stops at 2222.2222.2222.00-59 leaves a gap after the second entry, and a set that jumps from 1111.1111.1111.00-59 to 2222.2222.2222.00-00 leaves a gap between the first and second entry. Although it is legal to send a CSNP which contains no actual LSP entry TLVs, it should never be necessary to do so in order to conform to the specification.

Finally, the overload bit. To deal with transient problems that prevent a router from storing all the LSPs it receives, ISO 10589 defines an LSP Database Overload condition, in which the router sets a flag called the Overload Bit in the non-pseudonode LSP number zero that it generates. Other systems are instructed not to use an overloaded router as a transit router, since it does not have complete information, may not be able to compute the right routes, and routing loops could develop. An overloaded router might nonetheless become the DIS, so an implementation should not set the Overload bit in pseudo-node LSPs that it generates, and Overload bits seen in pseudo-node LSPs should be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: When routers exchange summaries of their link state, the summaries have to cover the whole range of possible identifiers, not just the ones this router happens to know about, or some updates get missed. And a router that has lost track of some routes should not be used to carry traffic through it.
